memoryText: And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Today there is no new reading. Today is for review and reflection on what you have learned in Unit 3.

Begin by memorizing the verse above if you have not already. Genesis 15:6 is the foundational verse of the doctrine of justification by faith. It is the verse Paul will quote in Romans 4 and Galatians 3 as the proof that justification has always been by faith, never by works of the law. Abraham believed God, and God counted it to him as righteousness. The transaction was simple, and it is the same transaction by which every Christian is justified today.

Say this verse aloud several times. Notice three things. First, Abraham believed. He did not earn, achieve, perform, or negotiate. He believed. Second, God counted it. The accounting is divine. God moves something from heaven’s ledger into Abraham’s account. Third, what God counted was righteousness. Not credit toward future righteousness. Not the possibility of righteousness. Righteousness itself. Abraham, who had lied about his wife, who had taken Hagar instead of waiting, who would lie again, Abraham was reckoned righteous because he believed.

This is your verse too if you are in Christ. You have believed. God has counted Christ’s righteousness to you. You are reckoned righteous before the throne. Not because of your performance. Because you believed.
unitRecap:
In Unit 3 you have traveled through Genesis 12 to 50, the entire patriarchal narrative. The unit began with the call of Abram, the great narrowing of God’s redemptive plan to one man and one family through whom all nations would be blessed. You followed Abraham through his call, his journey, his lies, his rescue of Lot, his meeting with Melchizedek, the formal cutting of the covenant in Genesis 15, the institution of circumcision, the long-awaited birth of Isaac, and the binding of Isaac on Mount Moriah.

Along the way, the plan paused for the doctrine of Covenant Theology, naming the structure that runs throughout the Bible. Five covenants, one unfolding story, all fulfilled in Christ.

The unit then continued through Isaac’s quieter life, Jacob’s deception and flight, his vision of the ladder at Bethel, his twenty years with Laban, the formation of the twelve tribes through Leah, Rachel, and the maidservants, his wrestling with God at Peniel, his reconciliation with Esau, and the renewal of the covenant at Bethel.

The Joseph narrative dominated the second half of the unit. Joseph sold by his brothers, falsely accused by Potiphar’s wife, forgotten in prison, finally elevated to second in command over Egypt, reuniting with his brothers, and forgiving them with the great theological summary: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”

The unit closed with Jacob’s death, his blessing of Judah (the scepter that would not depart), and Joseph’s bones in a coffin in Egypt, awaiting the Exodus to come.

The Psalms accompanied the journey: Psalm 105 in two parts, summarizing the patriarchal story in song; Psalm 121 and the Psalms of Ascent, teaching us to walk by faith; Psalm 37, the wisdom of patience under apparent injustice; Psalm 47 and Psalm 66, the universal kingship of God over all nations.

The big theological lessons of this unit are these: God’s covenant operates by election and grace, not by birth order or merit. Justification has always been by faith. God’s promises take time, sometimes decades, and they are fulfilled in his way, not ours. God’s providence works behind every event of human history, including the wickedness of others. And the line of Judah, the kingly tribe, runs all the way from Genesis 49 to Christ, the Lion of Judah, in whom every patriarchal promise finds its yes.

reviewQuestions.question: What are the three elements of God’s promise to Abraham, and how does each find fulfillment in Christ?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Read Genesis 12:1-3 again. The three elements are land, offspring (a great nation), and universal blessing (all families of the earth blessed). Each finds fulfillment in Christ: the land is fulfilled in the new heavens and new earth, the offspring is fulfilled in Christ himself (Galatians 3:16, “to Abraham and to his offspring… who is Christ”), and the universal blessing is fulfilled in the gospel going to every nation. Write a few sentences in your own words about how the gospel today fulfills each element of God’s promise to Abraham.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the covenant cutting of Genesis 15 reveal about the nature of God’s grace?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look back at Genesis 15. In the ancient Near East, both parties to a covenant walked between the cut pieces, pledging by self-curse to keep the covenant. But in Genesis 15, only God walks between the pieces. The covenant is one-sided. God binds himself to keep what he has promised, regardless of Abram’s faithfulness. This is grace in its purest form, God taking on himself the entire weight of the covenant. Centuries later, Christ on the cross was torn like the animals in Genesis 15, bearing the curse so that God’s people could be blessed. Sit with this. What does it mean for your assurance that God’s covenant with you depends on his faithfulness, not yours?

reviewQuestions.question: How does the story of Joseph function as a type of Christ?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Walk through Joseph’s life. He was the beloved son of his father (Genesis 37:3). He was hated and rejected by his brothers (37:4). He was sold for silver (37:28). He was wrongly accused and condemned (39:14-20). He was raised from the prison and given a name above every name in Egypt (41:39-43). He saved his brothers, including those who had sold him, by his elevation. He forgave them and provided for them. Every detail anticipates Christ. Take a moment to consider: in what specific ways did Joseph’s suffering and exaltation point forward to Jesus’ death and resurrection?

reviewQuestions.question: What does it mean that Abraham “believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness”?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Genesis 15:6, the most important Old Testament verse for understanding the New Testament’s doctrine of salvation. Three things are happening here. First, Abraham believed, faith is the means of justification, not works. Second, God counted, the accounting is divine, not earned. Third, what was counted was righteousness, Abraham was reckoned righteous before God on the basis of faith alone, not on the basis of his moral performance (which had already failed and would fail again). Paul will use this verse in Romans 4 to prove that justification has always been by faith. If you have believed in Christ, this is true of you too. Pray through this. Thank God that you are reckoned righteous, not because of who you are, but because of who Christ is.

prayerPrompts: Thank God for keeping his promise to Abraham when no one else could.
Thank him that you are a child of Abraham through faith in Christ.
Ask him to keep the unit verse in front of you.
